name: Núi Bà Đen (Black Virgin Mountain)
alternateNames: "Sun Mountain" (as Larry may have called it)
summary: An isolated mountain rising from the plain near Tây Ninh in southern Vietnam, site of significant U.S. military activity including a signal and relay presence on its summit. Larry's association became much more specific in his 2026-08-13 comments: he stood search-and-rescue duty at the Special Forces camp there — call sign Body Jab 42 — near the old French fort, photographed a rocket launcher being mounted on the summit (VN-0006), remembers Sgt. Lowry stationed on top, and places the "450 civilians" accusation here at the very end of his tour.
researchNotes: The mountain's location is settled geography; what remains unverified is the nature and dates of Larry's association with it. His 2026-08-13 testimony adds corroborating texture — the French fort matches the mountain's documented colonial ruins, and the two green berets visible in VN-0006 match the Special Forces presence he describes — but the photo's location is itself his identification, so the classification stays as recollection pending documentary support. The "Sun Mountain" name should be checked against period American nicknames. Special Forces and signal activity on the summit during 1964-1965 should be researched, including any Sergeant Lowry/Lowery and the camp call sign Body Jab 42 (see research/events/450-civilians-nui-ba-den.md). Research sweep 2026-08-13: the official Army history (Kelly, U.S. Army Special Forces 1961–1971) documents a CIDG camp at Núi Bà Đen itself in October 1964 manned by a half-size SF element — 1 officer, 5 enlisted, ~175 CIDG strikers — matching Larry's memory of a skeleton crew; the summit was taken by SF helicopter assault in May 1964, Detachment B-32 ran Tây Ninh province from January 1965, and the well-known 121st Signal Battalion relay ('Granite Romeo Tango') only arrived February 1966, so Larry's radio-relay window falls in the sparsely documented SF-relay period. 'French Fort on the back side of Nui Ba Den' is attested verbatim as an American place name. On this documentary fit the association is upgraded to plausible; direct confirmation of Larry's presence awaits his NPRC records. Archive session 2026-09-01 (research/places/nui-ba-den-locations.md): a veteran-compiled index of American positions, built from unit reports (sources/kindred-fsb-lz-index), gives the Special Forces camp here a designation and a date for the first time — Detachment A-324 (with A-325A also listed), opened July 1964, at grid XT281582 on 1:50,000 map sheet 6231-4 — and independently describes the summit as a Special Forces radio relay in that period, which is the part of the record that had been thinnest. Future records requests can now name Det A-324 rather than describe the camp. The same index also shows a cluster of positions on that sheet all called “French Fort,” around XT274686–XT289689 some eleven kilometres north of the summit — one prominent colonial work known to every American unit that passed through, occupied and renamed repeatedly between 1966 and 1971. It is recorded as a candidate for the fort Larry describes and not as an identification: the index is built from U.S. unit reports of 1966 and later, so a smaller ruin at the mountain’s base used by a half A-team in 1964–65 could be absent from it altogether. The 1:25,000 Pictomap sheets for 6231-4, which the archive supplies on request, should show fortification symbols directly and settle it. A photograph in a 5th Special Forces Group veteran's collection at the Library of Congress (sources/loc-vhp-chivers-nui-ba-den-1965) is captioned “Aerial view of Nui Ba Den (Black Lady) Mountain A-324 during air-drop, December 25, 1965” — the earliest independent use found of the designation by a man who served there rather than by a compiler, and, read with the rest of that collection, evidence that the summit was resupplied by air-drop.
